This is an interesting case. I'm curious if implementers find this particular user-story high priority enough (and high-frequency enough) to want to take on the implementation burden. It sounds like WebKit does!

Note that for blob URLs, this should already be accomplishable using a File. Quick demo: http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/?saved=5233. It appears nobody implements this, but that's a quality of implementation issue...

Given that, I'd personally prefer extending data URLs somehow, or just saying that you should use blob URLs if this user story is important for you.

Regardless, I'll ping some Blink folks to see if they're interested in the problem statement, leaving the solution aside for now. @smaug----, any thoughts from Gecko?
filename doesn't sound too bad. Use of blob uris would be rather awkward.
The solution should be per `<source>` too, as the format may differ.

Or per candidate URL? Do you want a different filename between URLs in `srcset`?

It would be possible to handle that by updating `img.filename` onload, and decide on filename from `currentSrc`. Annotating each `<source>` or each URL in a `<picture>` seems a bit annoying, but I dunno.

Per url in the `srcset` doesn't seem as important, as `kitten.jpg` should be fine for all of them. But in the case of `<source>` it could be `kitten.jpg` for one source and `kitten.webp` for another.

Updating `img.filename` dynamically would cover the use-case though.

This is an old suggestion, and I'm but a lowly web dev, but I'd love to see this implemented.  My use case is with dynamically created images.  While some are served straight through ``canvas`` elements, others are first converted to base64 data URIs in an ``img`` element in order to provide the plethora of options (copy link, e-mail, print, set as desktop, etc.) associated with them, but not with canvas elements\*

The problem faced is already outlined - the default filename given appears nonsensical.  There's a few possible existing solutions given but not detailed as to why they are cumbersome or insufficient.  

- Using a BLOB: As mentioned, browsers aren't respecting the filename.  But even if fixed, this would only make it so that the image can be saved with a reasonable filename - sharing the image outside of the page would break as an external site  would not know what the BLOB is referring to.  
- Using ``name=image.png`` in the mediatype: did not work in browsers tested  
- Wrapping the image in an ``a`` tag: While this offers a "save link as" with the sensible filename given with ``download``, "save image as" still co-exists in context menus and other handlers, and continue to offer the nonsensical filename.  
- Using a serviceworker to rewrite the fetch request: Not only does this install a serviceworker for no other purposes, setting it up for dynamic content proved to be an exercise (in futility - but I largely blame my own lack of experience with serviceworkers for that).  
- Re-serve the data server-side: Because the filename taken looks no further than the ``filename`` part of ``filename?data=base64``, possibly the smoothest experience - but fraught with issues as it requires server side processing, with either multiple server-side files or accepting any filename to internally redirect to the appropriate server side processing page, incurs a traffic hit on both the client and server ends, and may not play nice with third party websites that accept the base64 data URI, but not cross-domain locations.

When a user initially asked why images being saved through the context menu on desktop were being saved as "index" (actually, their localized version thereof), and I checked what I needed to add to give it a more appropriate filename, I was surprised to find there was no such feature.
I'm sure it isn't requested often, and is generally not a big deal (just give it a new name in the save dialog, right?), but it is one of those UX things that make a product just a tad more polished (suggest e.g. "projectname date.png" by default); while, no doubt, introducing a whole host of potential gotchas.

\* to wit, such a feature as discussed here would also be applicable to ``canvas`` elements regardless of the draggable property, if I'm not mistaken.

Thank you for your consideration!

Am I missing something, or we still don't have this feature?

I had a coupe of questions:
* Presumably, we want to strip any kind of `\` and `/` from the filename and possibly others, is there already a spec language that kind of sanitizes what's a proper name?
* Is `filename` a good name for this attribute? I was thinking some other suggestions might be `saveAs` or `downloadAs` or something since that's the context in which this name would be used. What do people think?

See https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#as-a-download. We don't define it in detail and that seems okay as it's largely UI-facing and not an interop matter. We should probably abstract parts of that algorithm and reuse those parts for this.

(I wouldn't mind reusing `download` as the value space would be the same and it's hopefully clear from context that the behavior is a little different. Don't feel strongly about naming though.)

Thinking about this a bit more: - Browsers may want to allow the user to download the image in a different format to the original. Eg, the image is an AVIF, but the browser may offer a way to download it as a PNG (via transcoding if a PNG source isn't provided). - `` images can be saved too, and they have no original format. It feels like we want a way to provide the basename of the file, rather than the whole file. ```html ``` Now the browser can add its own extension depending on the format (`cat.png`, `dog.avif` etc). You could still allow `basename` on `` for art-direction cases, but you wouldn't need to add a `basename` for each source if it's just the format that's changing.

[I asked folks about this on Twitter](https://twitter.com/jaffathecake/status/1436254336078819340). Some notes from the responses: - Almost everyone assumed this would change the click action for an image. I don't know if this was because of how I worded it, or if it was because of how `download` works on links. - A lot of folks asked about which image would be downloaded if a picture/srcset was involved. A few were asking for the browser to let the user pick. I realise that isn't part of this proposal. - Someone raised the issue of `` - would it be possible to make a file that rendered as an image, but on download was a different file type that would be harmful. Browsers can already download harmful files, but maybe users place more trust in image downloading? - A few folks said it'd be great to offer 'human' file names, for cases where the CDN adds a lot of cruft to the file name. Or similar: graphing APIs where the data is in the querystring, but the url path is general. A similar suggestion was localising file names. - Folks suggested this should also be on `

I completely understand the reason for wanting to specify a filename for a dynamically created image.  Although I think wrapping it in an `<a>` makes more sense. But I can see why that might be tricky for some designs.

But for server-supplied images, isn't this the responsibility of the [`content-disposition`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Disposition) header? A server could send `Content-Disposition: inline; filename="filename.jpg` to specify the eventual filename.
@edent see the top post in this thread. It talks about dynamically created content, and why content-disposition isn't a great workaround.

> * A few folks said it'd be great to offer 'human' file names, for cases where the CDN adds a lot of cruft to the file name. A similar suggestion was localising file names.

That's exactly the use case I'm interested about in this feature :-)

> * Browsers can already download harmful files, but maybe users place more trust in image downloading?

I feel like I have a lot more trust in "right-click, save image as..." to save an actual image as opposed to something like `.exe`. I don't have any such trust in `<a download>`. I like your `basename` proposal for this reason -- just let the browser pick the extension 

> * A few folks saying, if they intended a generated image to be downloadable, they'd just use `<a download>`.

I do wonder if this feature would be used. I imagine if the developer intended the image to be saved, they would have provided a way to click something that initiates the download. I don't know who would be optimizing for the case of users right-clicking and saving images. I'm sure those cases exist, but I can't imagine they are that widespread

> I'm sure those cases exist, but I can't imagine they are that widespread

They could start using it if it's provided, like for example using the image ALT field as the `basename` field, or the image title, or something more descriptive, so when downloading the image you don't get a hash... I know probably developers would not worry about people downloading images since they are already trying to prevent it (unsuccesfully if you try hard on getting them), but if it starts considered a best practice, maybe they change of mind... :-)

Note that with `<a download>` the browser gets to pick the extension as well (or ban certain extensions). See the processing model I linked. I don't think that should be a reason to use a different name.

One more motivation for providing a download name for data URIs and objectURLs:

On mobile browsers, the UX flow when saving images from `<a download>` is not as friendly as with long-pressing the image. On Chrome Android, you get a dual download dialog: one for the `a` and one for the `img`. On mobile Safari, long-press stops working and a tap gets you a very generic download dialog that asks to save the image into iTunes U.

Long-pressing an image not wrapped in an `a` gives you a friendly dialog to save the image to photos etc. but the download filename is an objectURL.

> Someone raised the issue of `` - would it be possible to make a file that rendered as an image, but on download was a different file type that would be harmful. Browsers can already download harmful files, but maybe users place more trust in image downloading? Technically that's still possible to do in browsers right now with the server sending `content-disposition` header with `filename=image.exe` ?

I came here because of this problem. Downloading an image on iOS Safari using `<a download>` is currently a very bad experience vs using long press and save to photos (e.g. in our case generating a profile image in our web app to download to a device then upload to a Twitter profile).

I also want to add that `<a download>` is worse UX on desktop, because with many browser configurations it automatically goes to the common downloads folder instead of letting you pick or automatically using the saved pictures folder which "save image" does.
